extracted.intended_audience: statesmen, politicians, political theorists, and educated readers interested in the English constitution and practical governance
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and practical standards about how Cabinet government, the House of Lords, the House of Commons, and leading statesmen ought to behave in the working English Constitution (mid-19th century context). Emphasises prerequisites for cabinet government, how to select and discuss political issues, and when institutions should yield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite: deferential electorate for Cabinet government
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabinet government is possible in England because England was a deferential country; the nominal constituency was not the real constituency and electors deferred to their 'betters'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bagehot argues that the mass of electors (e.g., the ten-pound householders) did not form independent political judgments but were guided by better educated classes; this deference was the only way the old system could be maintained and is therefore a political prerequisite for Cabinet government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statesmen must guide the new electorate quietly and responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: With the widening of the franchise, leading statesmen have the duty and opportunity to guide new voters in the exercise of the franchise—'to guide them quietly, and without saying what they are doing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ignorant or newly enfranchised voters are easily misled, statesmen should set the programme and settle which questions the public should attend to; they must provide direction without pedantic lecturing, using clear conclusions and light illustration so the press and public can follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select political issues with great care (avoid topics likely to mislead lower orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statesmen should avoid raising questions which will excite the lower orders on issues where their likely judgment would be wrong or antagonistic to the whole interest of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not propose topics that will bind the poor as a class together or that encourage the belief that new laws can create effortless comfort; prefer issues that lead to 'good issues' for the electorate and avoid those that foment class antagonism or false expectations of inexhaustible public funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering or bidding for the working-class vote
rubrics_metrics.description: Both parties bidding for the support of the working man by promising to do as he likes is corrupting and dangerous—'Vox populi will be Vox diaboli if it is worked in that manner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should not compete merely to defer to the decisions of uneducated majorities; doing so is politically corrupting and risks making popular will a malign force. Leaders must resist pressures to pander and instead responsibly shape issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide succinct, manly utterances rather than pedantic exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: What is mostly needed is the manly utterance of clear conclusions; lengthy formal exposition or a pedantic tone should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statesmen should communicate clear conclusions with a few light or humorous illustrations; a formal lecturing tone repels English audiences and signals inability to guide, whereas concise statements allow the press to disseminate the message effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let public perturbation entirely determine policy in excited times
rubrics_metrics.description: In excited times statesmen have scarcely any discretion; in quiet times they should use their large discretion to choose what fires to light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When public passion is high, leaders cannot freely choose topics; but when the mood is calm, they carry special responsibility to avoid initiating issues that will provoke dangerous popular combinations or long-term harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fighting losing battles that teach opponents to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in and especially losing protracted conflicts may teach the lower orders to organise and combine, thereby strengthening them in ways harmful to the existing constitutional balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage that yields a well-fought loss can be politically disastrous; leaders should recognise when contesting an issue will have the unintended effect of politically educating and organising the opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Lords should yield when Commons expresses the nation's will
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Lords ought to yield whenever the opinion of the Commons is also the opinion of the nation and it is clear that the nation has made up its mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining whether the nation is resolved must be judged by all circumstances (majorities, repeated passages, the unanimity of organs conveying opinion), not by a strict mechanical rule; if opinion is strong and varied, the Lords should yield at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use fixed mechanical tests for when Lords must yield
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal rule such as 'if the Commons pass a bill several times the nation is determined' is dangerous and misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important practical questions cannot be uniformly settled by fixed formulas; reliance on mechanical tests could justify obstinate resistance (e.g., the Lords rejecting the 1832 Reform) and risk revolution. Use a practical, circumstantial judgment instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: On great or 'first-class' subjects, Lords should be very slow to reject bills passed by large Commons majorities
rubrics_metrics.description: For important subjects the Lords should be slow—very slow—in rejecting a Bill passed even once by a large majority of the House of Commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an approximate practical rule (not unvarying): when Commons majorities genuinely reflect both representatives and constituencies, the Lords' resistance should be minimal to avoid dividing the educated classes and weakening their common resistance to uneducated majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dissension between Lords and Commons to maintain united resistance to uneducated majorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissension between the Lords and Commons divides the resisting power of the educated rich and is likely to benefit the uneducated majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since both Houses now largely represent different elements of the educated rich (plutocracy vs aristocracy), they should not bid against each other for popular support; unity preserves influence and prevents empowering uneducated combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Lords should exercise its power timidly and cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: The great power of the House of Lords should be exercised very timidly and very cautiously to keep their headship of the plutocracy and their broader influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peers should concede many points, even large ones if necessary, rather than endanger their overall position; minor and even some major concessions may preserve their substantive power. Practical measures (e.g., generous charitable giving) that maintain social capital are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove not only actual grievances but appearances of grievance
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher classes must avoid not only every actual evil but every appearance of evil; they must willingly concede every claim which they can safely concede to avert organised demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent the formation of permanent class combinations among the lower orders, elites should proactively address grievances and perceptions of injustice so popular anger has little rallying cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious in attributing immediate effects to reform Acts; allow time to see consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: It is too soon to estimate fully the effects of a major Reform Act immediately after its passage; political changes often reveal themselves only over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New constitutions or franchise reforms do not produce full effects as long as statesmen and electors are trained under the old system; one must wait until new generations and practices have had time to operate before judging consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the distorting effect of charismatic leaders on democratic tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal popularity (e.g., Gladstone's) can dominate elections, making it hard to assess how a new electorate will act absent such charisma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume election outcomes under an extraordinary personal influence reflect the steady working of a newly enfranchised system; such singular factors can mask underlying tendencies and mislead policy.
